newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-Lenzing mired in red, scraps 1996 dividend.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lenzing mired in red, scraps 1996 dividend.

text.p: Austrian fibre maker Lenzing AG announced on Thursday it was scrapping its dividend for 1996 and blamed an international price collapse for pushing the group deep into the red last year.

The firm, among the biggest producers of viscose and modal fibre, forecast another set of dismal results in 1997 but held out the hope that previously announced restructuring measures would bear fruit from 1998 onwards.

"1996 was one of the most difficult years in the history of the Lenzing group. International textile fibre markets suffered from considerable price reductions and a significant downturn in demand for viscose fibres," Lenzing said in a statement.

It reported a group net loss of 157.4 million schillings ($13.2 million) for 1996, compared with a 253.7 million schillings net profit the previous year, and a pre-tax loss of 30.3 million schillings versus a 1996 profit of 312.6 million.
Turnover fell to 7.786 billion schillings from 8.7 billion.
"As market conditions remain difficult, the executive board does not intend to propose a dividend for 1996," the firm said.
For 1995 Lenzing paid a 10 schillings dividend.

Lenzing shares slumped 22.9 schillings, or 3.27 percent, to 677 in Vienna making the stock by far the leading decliner in a generally soft market. Traders said the results had sparked "little excitement" among investors.
Analysts noted Lenzing's poor results were in stark contrast to the modest pre-tax profit rise announced by British rival Courtaulds Plc on Wednesday.
"Courtaulds came out with better figures while Lenzing has become mired in the red," said an international analyst, who declined to be named.
The group reported stormy times in all its key markets.
Troubled U.S. unit Lenzing Fibers Corp (LFC) suffered substantial losses in 1996 and required subordinated loans from the Austrian parent.
"As a precautionary measure, adjustments were made in Lenzing AG's 1996 balance sheet for all loans already granted to LFC and the book value of LFC," Lenzing said.
In Asia, associate company South Pacific Viscose posted a first-half loss for the first time in its history and in Europe prices for standard viscose fibres fell to 1980 levels.
Lenzing forecast a turbulent 1997 for its operations in Asia and the United States against a backdrop of polyester overcapacity and good cotton supplies.
"Because of lasting market weakness we do not expect an improvement in group results in 1997," the statement said. "The financial effects of internal measures will not take full effect until 1998."
Lenzing announced last year it would cut 500 jobs at its main Austrian production site and implement savings of 500 million schillings annually.

"The initial effects of this project will become evident in 1997, although as a result of one-off charges for restructuring, substantial benefits will not be seen until 1998," the company said. ($ = 11.93 Austrian Schillings)
